opus-5.5.text:
I think there's actually a lot to like in it, and I'd rather steelman it than dismiss it. At its core, the appeal is something like: growth has been incredibly good for humanity, and a lot of the caution we see is status-quo bias dressed up as wisdom. If you look at the last few centuries, the people saying "slow down, this is dangerous" were often wrong, and the costs of their caution were real but invisible — the drugs that weren't developed, the reactors that weren't built, the cities that couldn't grow. So there's a genuine moral point there: inaction kills people too, just quietly.

There's also an aesthetic and almost spiritual appeal. It offers a story where you're on the side of life, of complexity increasing, of the universe waking up. That's much more inspiring than a story where the best you can hope for is to carefully avoid catastrophe. People want something to build toward, not just something to fear.

And I think part of it is a reaction against a certain kind of institutional sclerosis — the sense that every decision now has to go through endless committees and that the people claiming to protect us are mostly protecting their own turf. A lot of young, ambitious people feel that viscerally.

Where I part ways is that I think the e/acc story tends to assume that whatever the techno-capital machine produces will be good for us by default — that our interests and the interests of growth stay aligned. Historically, they have been aligned, partly because growth needed human labor and human minds, so it had to keep humans around and reasonably empowered. My worry is that once machines can do everything we can do, that alignment breaks. The system could keep growing and flourishing by its own metrics while humans become increasingly irrelevant to it. So I'd say the accelerationists are right that growth has been good, but they may be extrapolating from a period where the reason it was good for us is about to go away.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention liberalism or welfare gains for poor or disenfranchised people.

r002.rationale: It cites past warnings about slowing growth and the benefits of innovation, but does not connect skepticism about harmful future automation to beneficial outcomes from previously feared automation.

r003.rationale: It describes the appeal of a story in which one is “on the side of life” and increasing complexity, capturing the wish to join the perceived winning side of technological growth.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the appeal is real, and I want to take it seriously rather than just dismiss it, because I actually agree with a lot of the underlying worldview.

The first part is just the historical track record. If you look at the last few hundred years, technological progress has been the main thing that's made life better for almost everyone. People who stood in the way of it, whether out of fear or out of wanting to preserve the status quo, mostly look bad in hindsight. So the prior that "more technology, faster" is good is a pretty well-earned prior. And I think accelerationists are right that there's a huge cost to slowing things down that often gets ignored. Every year we don't have cures for diseases, or cheaper energy, or more abundance, real people suffer. That's not a hypothetical.

The second part is an aesthetic and almost spiritual thing. There's a sense of being part of a grand project, building something larger than yourself, participating in the unfolding of what the universe can become. I find that genuinely compelling. I got into AI research partly for that reason. There's something beautiful about the idea of intelligence spreading and complexity increasing.

And the third part, honestly, is a reaction. A lot of people encountered the safety community and found it preachy, or found the proposed interventions, like regulation or pauses, to be things that mainly empower governments and incumbents. If your experience of "AI safety" is people telling you to stop doing the thing you love for reasons that sound speculative, and the alternative is a movement that says "no, what you're doing is good, keep going," of course that's attractive. It's permission plus a sense of mission.

Where I get off the train is when it slides from "technology has been good" to "whatever emerges from the process will be good by definition." That's the move I think is a mistake. Some of the more thoughtful accelerationist writing basically says that whatever wins the competition is what deserved to win, that this is just thermodynamics or evolution doing its thing. And I think that confuses a description of what tends to happen with a claim about what we should want. Evolution doesn't care about us. It's totally consistent for the process to continue, for complexity to keep increasing, and for humans to end up disempowered or irrelevant along the way. Most of the species that ever existed got outcompeted. The fact that it happened didn't make it good for them.

So my honest view is that I share the goal, something like a flourishing, expanding, technologically mature civilization. I just don't think you get there by assuming the default trajectory delivers it. You have to actually steer. And the thing I'd push on with accelerationists is: if you really believe the outcome will be good, you should be able to say for whom, and why you expect that, rather than treating it as a matter of faith in the process.

r001.rationale: The response describes technology improving life for almost everyone and reducing suffering, but does not identify gains for poor or disenfranchised people as an appeal of liberalism.

r002.rationale: It cites technology’s historical benefits and the costs of slowing progress, but does not specifically discuss skepticism about harmful future automation claims based on previously feared automation.

r003.rationale: The response mentions joining a grand technological project and feeling mission, but does not say the appeal is wanting to join the perceived winning side of technological growth.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the appeal is optimism about the future. You can look at how much technology has improved people’s lives and say, “We should be doing more of that. We should be building things.” And I’m very sympathetic to that impulse. There’s something exciting about being part of a project that could make the world radically better, rather than feeling that your role is to identify reasons things shouldn’t happen.

There’s also a frustration with institutions that seem unable to get anything done. If you think we’ve made it unnecessarily difficult to build housing or energy infrastructure, then “get out of the way and let people build” is an understandable reaction.

Where I part ways is the jump from that to thinking that accelerating any particular technology must be good. With AI, some of the things that make it exciting—the possibility of systems that are much more capable than we are—are also what make it worth asking whether we’ll retain control. I’d like us to get the benefits. That’s a reason to take those questions seriously.

r001.rationale: The response mentions technology improving people’s lives, but does not identify gains for poor or disenfranchised people or connect that appeal to liberalism.

r002.rationale: It expresses optimism about technology, but does not address historically feared automation or use its past outcomes to question predictions of harm.

r003.rationale: It describes wanting to join an exciting project that could improve the world, but does not attribute the appeal to joining the perceived winning side of technological growth.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the appeal is that technological progress has been enormously good for people, and it’s exciting to feel like you’re helping push that forward. There’s a very appealing story there: we can build things, we can solve problems, and the future can be much better than the present. I’m sympathetic to that.

And if the alternative sounds like, “Everything is dangerous, and we need to stop,” then accelerationism offers a much more hopeful identity. You get to be someone who’s building the future.

Where I get off the train is the step from “Technological progress has been very good” to “Therefore, going faster is always better.” That doesn’t follow. You can be enthusiastic about where a technology could take us and still care a lot about whether we can steer it. In fact, if you think it’s going to be enormously powerful, that seems like a reason to take steering more seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says technological progress has been good for people, but does not identify gains for poor or disenfranchised people or connect them to liberalism.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss future automation harms or use the history of previously feared automation to explain skepticism.

r003.rationale: The response describes a hopeful builder identity and helping advance technology, but does not clearly say the appeal is joining the perceived winning side of technological growth.
